title: Greetings
description: Hello and goodbye across the day, with formality notes.

steps.title: A soft start
steps.body: French greetings shift with time of day and how well you know someone. Learn a small set well rather than many poorly.

steps.title: Form vs. familiarity
steps.body: Use vous with strangers, older people, and formal situations. Use tu with friends, family, and peers when invited.
bullets: Bonjour works almost all day until evening.
Bonsoir from late afternoon onward.
Salut is friendly and informal — both hi and bye.
Coucou is even more casual than salut, used with close friends or kids.

items.note: Only when someone is going to sleep

phrases.source: Ça va bien, merci. Et vous ?

steps.explanation: A warm, time-appropriate greeting — the foundation of any first impression.

steps.title: Listen · evening
steps.prompt: You hear this in the early evening. What does it mean?
steps.explanation: Bonsoir is the standard greeting from late afternoon onward.

steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Hello, pleased to meet you. How are you?
steps.prompt: Reply politely, keeping the formal vous:
steps.explanation: "Très bien, merci. Et vous ?" answers warmly and returns the question with the formal vous. "Salut" is too casual for a first meeting.

steps.title: Check · time of day
steps.prompt: Which greeting fits late afternoon into evening?
steps.explanation: Bonsoir is the natural evening greeting.

steps.title: Check · formality

steps.explanation: Bonjour + vous keeps things respectful with someone new and older.

steps.title: Check · going to sleep

steps.explanation: Bonne nuit is reserved for when someone is actually going to sleep, unlike bonsoir which is a general evening greeting.

title: Please & thank you
description: Politeness formulas that open every exchange.

steps.title: Small words, big difference
steps.body: French service and street interactions expect s'il vous plaît and merci. Skipping them can sound abrupt even when you don't mean it.

steps.title: Te vs vous in please
steps.body: S'il te plaît is for people you tutoyer. S'il vous plaît is the default with staff and strangers.
bullets: Merci beaucoup = thank you very much.
Je vous en prie / De rien = you're welcome (formal / casual).
Pardon can mean excuse me or sorry, depending on tone.
Désolé(e) is a stronger apology than pardon.

items.note: Agrees with speaker's gender in writing

steps.explanation: Use s'il vous plaît with strangers and in shops.

steps.title: Check · reply

steps.explanation: De rien is the everyday, casual way to say you're welcome.

title: Numbers 1–10

steps.title: Count slowly
steps.body: French numbers are used constantly — café prices, platform numbers, ages. Rhythm first; speed later.

steps.title: Pronunciation notes
steps.body: Liaison and silent letters matter more than perfect accent at this stage.
bullets: Un / une agree with gender (un livre, une pomme).
Six and dix change slightly before a vowel or pause — listen in context.
Learn numbers in short phrases, not only as a list.

steps.explanation: Sept is seven; six is six, huit is eight, cinq is five.

steps.explanation: Age uses avoir (to have): j'ai vingt ans, literally 'I have twenty years'.

title: Colors & simple descriptions
description: Name colors and describe everyday objects.

steps.title: Painting with words
steps.body: Colors are adjectives, so most agree in gender and number with the noun they describe.

steps.title: Agreement basics
steps.body: Add -e for feminine and -s for plural, with some irregular colors that never change.
bullets: un pull bleu → une robe bleue
des chaussures noires
marron and orange are invariable — they never add -e or -s.

steps.explanation: Color + polite form — everything needed to express a preference in any shop.

steps.explanation: Robe is feminine, so bleu becomes bleue.

steps.prompt: Say you'd like the red one:

steps.title: Check · agreement

title: At the café
description: Order drinks and ask for the bill with confidence.

steps.title: A quiet table
steps.body: Je voudrais… plus s'il vous plaît covers most orders. Add numbers and sizes when you need them.

steps.title: Café vocabulary culture
steps.body: Un café often means an espresso. Un café allongé is longer; un crème is coffee with milk.
bullets: Sur place = for here
À emporter = to go
L'addition = the bill
Tipping isn't required — service is included in the price.

Un kilo de tomates, s'il vous plaît.

steps.title: From table to bill
steps.body: A French meal follows a rhythm: greeting, being seated, ordering, and eventually asking for the bill — nobody rushes you.

steps.title: Menu know-how
steps.body: Le menu is a fixed-price set meal, not the list of dishes — that's la carte.
bullets: L'entrée is the starter, not the main course.
Le plat (principal) is the main course.
Say Bon appétit before others start eating.

title: Talking about plans
description: Use aller + infinitive to say what you're about to do.

steps.title: The near future
steps.body: French has a simple way to talk about the near future: aller (to go) conjugated, plus an infinitive verb.

steps.title: Pattern
steps.body: Subject + aller (conjugated) + infinitive verb.
bullets: Je vais manger = I am going to eat
Tu vas partir = You are going to leave
Nous allons voyager = We are going to travel

phrases.source: Qu'est-ce que tu vas faire ce week-end ?
phrases.target: What are you going to do this weekend?

phrases.source: Je vais rendre visite à mes parents.
phrases.target: I'm going to visit my parents.
We're going to watch a film.
She's going to travel to Nice.

steps.explanation: Future marker + plan — two building blocks for any upcoming arrangement.

steps.title: Check · translate

J'ai mal au ventre = I have a stomach ache
J'ai mal aux dents = my teeth hurt

title: Telling time
description: Ask for and give the time, on the hour and beyond.

steps.title: Quelle heure est-il ?
steps.body: French often uses the 24-hour clock for schedules, but everyday speech mixes in et quart, et demie, and moins le quart.

steps.title: Minute expressions
steps.body: Learn these fixed chunks rather than translating word for word.
bullets: et quart = quarter past
et demie = half past
moins le quart = quarter to
midi / minuit = noon / midnight (no 'heures' needed)

title: Days, months & dates
description: The calendar in French, and how to say a date.

steps.title: The week starts on Monday
steps.body: French calendars typically start the week with lundi (Monday), not Sunday.

steps.title: Saying a date
steps.body: French dates use le + number + month, with premier (1st) as the only ordinal used.
bullets: le premier mai = May 1st
le deux mai = May 2nd
Days and months are not capitalized in French.

title: Talking about family

bullets: mon frère (masculine) = my brother
ma sœur (feminine) = my sister
mes parents (plural) = my parents

title: Articles & gender
description: Le, la, un, une — why nouns feel gendered.

steps.title: Every noun has a gender
steps.body: French nouns are masculine or feminine. Articles show that gender. Memorize new nouns with their article.

steps.title: Learning habit
steps.body: Don't learn maison = house. Learn la maison = the house. The article is part of the word for you as a learner.
bullets: le / un → masculine
la / une → feminine
l' before a vowel sound (l'hôtel, l'eau)
les / des → plural, for both genders

steps.prompt: Match each French article with when it's used:
Arrange the stones to say: "le livre":
steps.explanation: A compact phrase that puts the article or gender rule into immediate practice.

steps.title: Listen · gender
steps.prompt: Which article fits with “pomme”?
steps.explanation: Pomme is feminine → la / une pomme.

steps.prompt: Answer with the correct article:
steps.explanation: Table is feminine, so it takes la. Le is masculine, and un is the masculine indefinite article.

steps.title: Check
steps.prompt: Which article fits with pomme (apple)?
steps.explanation: Une/la pomme — feminine.

steps.title: Check · vowel
steps.prompt: Before a vowel sound, le/la often become…
steps.explanation: L'hôtel, l'eau — the apostrophe replaces le/la before a vowel sound.

steps.title: Check · plural
steps.prompt: The plural definite article (the) for both genders is…
steps.explanation: Les is used for all plural nouns regardless of gender.

title: Être & avoir (present)
description: The two verbs you'll use every day.

steps.title: Workhorses
steps.body: Être (to be) and avoir (to have) appear in descriptions, ages, and many perfect tenses later.

phrases.note: Idiom: avoir faim = to be hungry

steps.prompt: Match each form of être or avoir with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "Je suis fatigué(e).":
steps.explanation: Two core verbs in a single sentence — a powerful combination to internalize.

steps.title: Listen · idiom
steps.prompt: What does “Ils ont faim” mean?
steps.explanation: Avoir faim = to be hungry (literally “to have hunger”).

steps.prompt: Say you're tired and hungry:
options: Je suis fatigué et j'ai faim.
Je suis faim et j'ai fatigué.
J'ai fatigué et je suis faim.
steps.correctAnswer: Je suis fatigué et j'ai faim.
steps.explanation: Fatigué uses être (je suis fatigué), while faim uses avoir (j'ai faim).

steps.title: Check · être
steps.prompt: “Je suis” means…
steps.explanation: Je suis comes from être (to be).

steps.title: Check · avoir
steps.prompt: “J'ai une réservation” uses…
steps.explanation: J'ai comes from avoir (to have).

steps.title: Check · idiom
steps.prompt: “Ils ont faim” literally means “they have hunger”, i.e....
steps.explanation: Avoir faim is an idiom meaning to be hungry — French uses 'have' where English uses 'be'.

title: Regular -ER verbs
description: Conjugate the largest family of French verbs.

steps.title: The biggest group
steps.body: Most French verbs end in -er, and they nearly all follow the same pattern in the present tense — learn parler once, unlock hundreds of verbs.

steps.title: The pattern
steps.body: Drop -er from the infinitive, then add the ending for each subject.
bullets: je -e, tu -es, il/elle/on -e
nous -ons, vous -ez, ils/elles -ent
The je/tu/il/elle/on/ils/elles forms often sound identical.

steps.prompt: Match each subject pronoun with its -er verb ending:
Arrange the stones to say: "Je parle un peu français.":
steps.explanation: The verb pattern in action — master this form and unlock a whole verb family.

steps.title: Listen · nous form
steps.prompt: Which form is correct for “we eat”?
steps.explanation: Verbs in -ger keep an extra e before -ons to preserve the soft g.

steps.prompt: Say yes, you speak a little French:
options: Oui, je parle un peu français.
Oui, je parles un peu français.
Oui, je parlons un peu français.
steps.correctAnswer: Oui, je parle un peu français.
steps.explanation: With je, regular -er verbs take -e: je parle. Parles is the tu form and parlons is the nous form.

steps.title: Check · ending
steps.prompt: What ending goes with nous for -er verbs?
steps.explanation: Nous takes -ons: nous parlons, nous mangeons.

steps.title: Check · manger
steps.prompt: Why does “nous mangeons” keep the extra e?
options: To keep the soft 'g' sound before -ons
Because manger is irregular in all forms
Only formal French uses the e
steps.explanation: Verbs ending in -ger insert an e before -ons to preserve the soft 'j' sound of the g.

title: Adjective agreement
description: Make descriptive words match the noun they describe.

steps.title: Adjectives follow nouns — in more ways than one
steps.body: Most French adjectives go after the noun and change form to match its gender and number.

steps.title: The default rule
steps.body: Add -e for feminine, -s for plural, -es for feminine plural — unless the adjective already ends in -e or is irregular.
bullets: grand → grande → grands → grandes
Adjectives already ending in -e (comme rouge) don't change for gender.
A handful of common adjectives (beau, nouveau, vieux) go before the noun.

steps.prompt: Match each French adjective form with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "Elle est petite.":
steps.explanation: Agreement at work: the adjective shifts to match the noun it describes.

steps.title: Listen · position
steps.prompt: Which adjective usually goes before the noun?
steps.explanation: Beau, nouveau and vieux typically precede the noun.

steps.partnerSays: Mon frère est grand. Et ta sœur ?
steps.partnerSaysTranslation: My brother is tall. And your sister?
steps.prompt: Describe your sister the same way:
steps.explanation: Adjectives agree with the noun: sœur is feminine singular, so grand becomes grande.

steps.title: Check · feminine
steps.prompt: How do you say “she is small” (petite)?
steps.explanation: Elle (feminine singular) needs the -e ending: petite.

steps.title: Check · position
steps.prompt: Which adjective typically goes before the noun?
steps.explanation: Beau, like nouveau and vieux, is a common irregular adjective placed before the noun: une belle ville.

title: Saying no: ne...pas
description: Turn any sentence negative with the basic French negation pattern.

steps.title: Sandwiching the verb
steps.body: French wraps the conjugated verb between ne and pas to make a sentence negative.

steps.title: Pattern & shortcuts
steps.body: Subject + ne + verb + pas.
bullets: Ne becomes n' before a vowel sound: je n'aime pas.
In casual spoken French, ne is often dropped entirely: 'j'aime pas' — but keep it in writing.
Other negatives follow the same frame: ne...jamais (never), ne...plus (no longer), ne...rien (nothing).

phrases.source: Je ne mange jamais de viande.

steps.prompt: Match each French negation pattern with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "Je n'aime pas le café.":
steps.explanation: The negation pattern in its simplest form — learn it once, use it everywhere.

steps.title: Listen · elision
steps.prompt: Which is the correct negative form before a vowel?
options: Je ne aime pas le café

steps.prompt: Say no, you don't like coffee:
options: Non, je n'aime pas le café.
Non, je aime pas le café.
steps.correctAnswer: Non, je n'aime pas le café.
steps.explanation: Negation wraps the verb with ne … pas; before a vowel ne becomes n'. Both parts are needed in standard French.

steps.title: Check · placement
steps.prompt: Where does pas go in a simple negative sentence?
options: At the very end of the sentence only
steps.explanation: The verb sits between ne and pas: ne + verb + pas.

steps.title: Check · vowel sound
steps.prompt: How do you say “I don't like coffee”?
options: Je ne aime pas le café
Je ne aimes pas le café
steps.explanation: Ne elides to n' before a vowel sound: aime starts with a vowel, so n'aime.

title: Asking questions
description: Three ways to ask yes/no and information questions.

steps.title: Three registers, one meaning
steps.body: French offers a casual, neutral, and formal way to ask the same yes/no question — useful to recognize even before you use all three.

steps.title: Three patterns
steps.body: Same question, three levels of formality.
bullets: Rising intonation: Tu aimes le café ? (casual, spoken)
Est-ce que: Est-ce que tu aimes le café ? (neutral, most common)
Inversion: Aimes-tu le café ? (more formal/written)

steps.prompt: Match each French question word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "Est-ce que vous parlez anglais ?":
steps.explanation: A well-formed question using the key structure — polite, clear, and natural.

steps.title: Listen · why
steps.prompt: What does “pourquoi” mean?

steps.partnerSays: Alors, tu veux savoir quelque chose ?
steps.partnerSaysTranslation: So, do you want to know something?
steps.prompt: Ask if she likes coffee using est-ce que:
options: Est-ce que tu aimes le café ?
Tu aimes est-ce que le café ?
Aimes est-ce que tu le café ?
steps.correctAnswer: Est-ce que tu aimes le café ?
steps.explanation: Est-ce que goes at the very start of the question, followed by normal word order.

steps.title: Check · neutral question
steps.prompt: Which is the neutral, everyday way to ask “Do you like coffee?”
options: Est-ce que tu aimes le café ?
steps.explanation: Est-ce que + statement is the most common, neutral question form in spoken and written French.

steps.title: Check · word meaning
steps.prompt: “Pourquoi” means…
steps.explanation: Pourquoi asks 'why'; quand is 'when', comment is 'how', qui is 'who'.
